question: What is the minimum age to legally operate a personal watercraft (PWC) designed for one person in California?
choice_c: There is no minimum age for a single-rider PWC
explanation: California requires a PWC operator to be at least 16 years old, with a narrow exception for supervised operation of a multi-person PWC.
source_note: CA PWC operating-age requirements (H&N Code / DBW/boat-ed CA course)

question: Under what condition may a 12- to 15-year-old legally operate a personal watercraft in California?
choice_a: The PWC is designed to carry two or more persons, and the minor is directly supervised on board by someone 18 or older
choice_b: Only if riding alone during daylight hours
choice_c: Only with a note from a parent, without anyone else aboard
choice_d: 12- to 15-year-olds may never operate a PWC under any circumstance
explanation: A 12- to 15-year-old may operate a PWC built for two or more riders only if directly supervised on board by an adult at least 18 years old.

question: What must every PWC operator equipped with an engine cutoff switch and lanyard do before operating?
choice_a: Attach the lanyard to the dock instead of themselves
choice_b: Attach the lanyard to their person, clothing, or life jacket
choice_c: Leave the lanyard disconnected to prevent accidental engine shutoff
choice_d: Only attach the lanyard while operating at idle speed
explanation: California law requires PWC operators to physically attach the engine cutoff lanyard to themselves so the engine stops automatically if they are thrown off.
source_note: CA PWC equipment law; federal ECOS requirement (33 CFR 175)

question: What life jacket rule applies to every person operating or riding on a PWC in California?
choice_a: A PFD only needs to be carried aboard, not worn
choice_b: PFDs are optional if the PWC has a cutoff lanyard
choice_c: Each person must wear a USCG-approved wearable PFD at all times
choice_d: Only the operator must wear a PFD; passengers do not need one
explanation: Every operator and passenger on a PWC must wear (not just carry) a USCG-approved wearable PFD.
source_note: Cal. Harbors & Navigation Code, PWC equipment provisions

question: How close may a PWC legally operate to a bather (a person in the water swimming) in California?
choice_a: PWCs may operate as close as they wish to bathers
choice_d: No closer than 100 feet, except at slow-no-wake speed on a direct course to launch or land
explanation: It is illegal to operate a PWC within 100 feet of a bather in California, except when proceeding at slow-no-wake speed on a direct route to or from shore.

question: During what hours is it illegal to operate a PWC on California waters?
choice_c: There are no hour restrictions on PWC operation
explanation: California prohibits PWC operation between sunset and sunrise, similar to restrictions on other high-speed watersports activities.

question: How close may a PWC operate to a designated swimming beach or a passenger-landing area in California?
choice_b: No closer than 200 feet, other than at slow-no-wake speed on a direct approach
choice_c: No restriction applies near beaches for PWCs specifically
explanation: PWCs, like other motorized vessels, must stay at least 200 feet from a beach or landing area used by swimmers or passengers, except at slow-no-wake speed while directly approaching or departing.

question: Why do PWC-specific rules (age minimums, lanyard use, distance limits) exist in addition to general boating rules?
choice_a: PWC rules exist purely to generate registration revenue
choice_b: There is no meaningful safety rationale behind PWC-specific rules
choice_c: PWCs are highly maneuverable, fast-accelerating craft frequently involved in collisions with swimmers, docks, and other vessels when operated carelessly
choice_d: PWCs are considered safer than other vessels, so extra rules are just precautionary
explanation: PWCs' quick acceleration, tight turning, and popularity for close-quarters recreation make them statistically over-represented in certain collision types, driving targeted regulations.
source_note: General PWC safety rationale, standard NASBLA-course content

question: Must a rented personal watercraft in California still comply with the same equipment and operating rules (PFDs, lanyard, distance, hours) as a privately owned PWC?
choice_a: No, rental PWCs are exempt from all state boating laws
choice_b: Only the lanyard rule applies to rentals
choice_c: Rental PWCs may be operated at any hour, day or night
choice_d: Yes -- rental status does not exempt a PWC from equipment or operating requirements
explanation: Whether privately owned or rented, a PWC operator must follow the same PFD, cutoff-lanyard, distance, and hours-of-operation rules.
source_note: General PWC rental compliance, CA boating law

question: If a PWC is towing a person on water skis or a tube, what additional equipment/personnel rule from California's general towing law also applies?
choice_a: An observer or an approved alternative (as allowed by law) must be able to monitor the person being towed, and a ski flag may be required to mark a person in the water
choice_b: Towing is completely banned from a PWC in California
choice_c: No additional rule applies beyond the standard PWC PFD rule
choice_d: Only the person being towed needs a PFD; the PWC operator does not
explanation: California's general towed-watersports rules -- including having someone able to observe the person being towed and displaying a ski flag for a person in the water -- apply on top of standard PWC equipment rules.
source_note: Cal. Harbors & Navigation Code, towing provisions applied to PWCs

question: What is a common, dangerous mistake new PWC operators make when trying to avoid a collision?
choice_a: Operating below the posted speed limit
choice_b: Releasing the throttle without also steering away, which can reduce or eliminate steering control on many PWC designs
choice_c: Steering too early, well before any hazard appears
choice_d: Wearing a PFD, which reduces reaction time
explanation: Many PWCs steer using directed thrust from the jet drive; releasing the throttle in a panic can reduce steering response exactly when a turn is needed most, so operators are taught to steer away while maintaining some throttle.
source_note: General PWC handling fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

question: What should a PWC operator do before getting underway, regarding the ignition safety (cutoff) lanyard?
choice_a: Store it in a dry bag for the duration of the ride
choice_b: Only attach it if operating in open ocean water
choice_c: Confirm it is properly attached to their body and functioning before leaving the dock or shore
choice_d: Remove it, since it can interfere with acceleration
explanation: Checking that the cutoff lanyard is properly attached and working before departure ensures the engine will stop automatically if the operator is separated from the PWC.
source_note: General PWC pre-departure checklist, standard NASBLA-course content

question: Can a PWC legally be operated at night with navigation lights installed, given California's sunset-to-sunrise PWC ban?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the PWC has functioning navigation lights
choice_b: Yes, but only on lakes, never on the ocean
choice_c: Yes, with no restriction at all
choice_d: No -- the sunset-to-sunrise operating ban applies to PWCs regardless of whether navigation lights are installed
explanation: Installing navigation lights does not override California's blanket sunset-to-sunrise prohibition on PWC operation.

question: What must a person do before operating a PWC in California under the general Boater Card mandate?
choice_a: Complete an approved boating safety course and obtain a California Boater Card, the same as any other motorized-vessel operator
choice_b: Nothing; PWCs are exempt from the Boater Card requirement
choice_c: Obtain a special PWC-only license issued by DBW directly
choice_d: Pass a road-based DMV driving test instead of a boating course
explanation: PWCs are motorized vessels, so their operators are fully subject to the same California Boater Card mandate as operators of any other motorboat.
